title: A systematic review of AI, VR, and LLM applications in special education: Opportunities, challenges, and future directions
extended_summary:
This paper addresses the rapidly expanding use of artificial intelligence (AI), virtual reality (VR), augmented reality (AR), and large language models (LLMs) in special education, with a focus on opportunities, challenges, and future directions. The review asks how these technologies are being used for students with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND), how they may be combined, what special education methodologies support their adoption, and what barriers remain for implementation and inclusion.

The authors conducted a systematic review and deductive thematic analysis of 139 studies retrieved from ArXiv and ScienceDirect. The paper synthesizes literature on VR/AR interventions, AI/LLM-based tools, teacher attitudes toward inclusion and technology, and syndrome-specific assistive applications spanning autism spectrum disorder, intellectual disabilities, down syndrome, visual and hearing impairments, learning disabilities, motor disabilities, speech impairments, and emotional/psychological disorders. The context is broad special education practice rather than a single intervention site, and the review considers both student-facing and teacher-facing uses of these technologies.

The main conclusion is that VR, AR, AI, and LLMs each show promise for personalized learning, engagement, communication, and accessibility, but evidence remains fragmented and largely theoretical with limited integrated frameworks for special education. The paper emphasizes unresolved issues including accessibility, bias, cybersecurity, privacy, cost, teacher preparedness, and the need for clearer policies and professional development. It concludes that future work should develop robust implementation frameworks and cross-sector collaboration to support equitable and effective use of these technologies in special education.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Generic large language model / generative AI chatbot or assistant used for language generation, question answering, feedback, personalization, and related educational support.
identified_tools.use_case: This systematic review synthesizes literature on LLMs and other AI/immersive technologies in special education, including uses such as tutoring, feedback, lesson-planning support, content generation, and adaptive communication. It does not evaluate one specific named product as the sole focus; instead it discusses heterogeneous LLM-based systems and applications.

findings.finding_summary: The review reports that LLMs and AI can support literacy-related tasks in special education, including simplifying complex texts into Easy-to-Read formats and supporting literacy learning through personalized, multimodal interaction. It also notes that some VR-based interventions were effective in literacy and language learning for students with ADHD, but the paper does not provide pooled effect sizes or controlled-study estimates.
findings.measure: Literacy and language learning outcomes; text simplification/accessibility for cognitive impairments

findings.finding_summary: The review concludes that AI/LLMs may enhance personalized learning, accessibility, inclusion, and teacher support in special education, but emphasizes major concerns about bias, safety, hallucinations/false information, privacy, and lack of validated frameworks. It highlights that teacher-AI collaboration may assist grading, progress tracking, content generation, and personalized feedback, while human oversight remains necessary.
findings.measure: Reported opportunities and challenges for AI/LLM use in special education

quality_tier_rationale: This is a systematic review synthesizing heterogeneous prior studies rather than a primary experimental evaluation. The evidence base is broad, but the paper reports thematic synthesis without pooled quantitative estimates for a single tool.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper suggests potentially meaningful benefits for literacy support and personalized learning, but the reported outcomes are qualitative and mixed, with no effect sizes or causal estimates. The practical impact is therefore promising but not quantifiable from this review.
